What the official sources say

  • Unlawful squatting (O.C.G.A. 16-7-21.1, enacted by HB 1017, effective Apr 24, 2024): entering and residing on another's land or premises without the owner's or rightful occupant's knowledge or consent is a misdemeanor. (HB 1017 (Georgia Squatter Reform Act), 16-7-21.1(a)-(b); source)
  • An accused squatter gets a citation and must show properly executed documentation (lease or proof of rent payments) to the issuing agency within 3 business days or is subject to arrest; if documentation is submitted, a hearing is set within 7 days. (HB 1017, 16-7-21.1(a)(2)-(4); source)
  • Owner removal of an intruder: affidavit of good-faith right of possession; the sheriff or certified officer turns the person out once 3 days have elapsed from exhibition of the affidavit, unless the occupant files a counteraffidavit, which sends both affidavits to court for trial. (HB 1017, O.C.G.A. 44-11-30 and 44-11-32 as revised; source)
  • If the court finds the occupant's counteraffidavit not meritorious by a preponderance, the occupant is removed under a writ of possession and the court may award fair market rent for the occupancy. (HB 1017, O.C.G.A. 44-11-32(a)(2)-(3); source)

Georgia Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Georgia house?

Check the statute and talk to a Georgia attorney about your facts.

Is squatting a crime in Georgia?

Yes. The Georgia Squatter Reform Act, House Bill 1017 of the 2024 session, created O.C.G.A. 16-7-21.1. A person commits unlawful squatting by entering the land or premises of another and residing there for any period of time, knowing the owner, rightful occupant or an authorized representative has not consented.

The statute defines residing simply as inhabiting or living on or within the land or premises. The offense is a misdemeanor punished under 17-10-3. The Act took effect when the governor approved it.

The same bill also changed the magistrate court's reach. The magistrate court may now try unlawful squatting violations and hear the owner's intruder proceedings under Code Sections 44-11-30 through 44-11-33.

What can an accused squatter do to avoid arrest?

Show paperwork. Anyone accused receives a citation telling them to present, within three business days, properly executed documentation authorizing their entry. The head of the issuing law enforcement agency, or a designee, is the person who receives it.

The statute names examples of acceptable documents: a properly executed lease or rental agreement, or proof of rental payments. A person who cannot produce anything is subject to arrest.

A person who does submit documents gets a hearing within seven days. If the court finds the documents were not properly executed or have no merit, that person can be subject to removal, arrest and penalties under 16-9-1 and 16-9-2, and an additional fine based on the fair market monthly rent of the property.

Who handles a squatting case, police or a court?

Both play a part. Law enforcement issues the citation that starts the three business day clock, and the head of that agency or a designee receives the occupant's documents. The courts take over if the paperwork is challenged: the bill gives the magistrate court authority to try unlawful squatting violations and to run the owner's intruder proceedings.

The bill's title also says proceedings on a writ of possession are not required to be jury trials. For an owner, the practical effect is a faster, more local forum than a full civil suit, since the magistrate court sits in the county where the property is.

How does an owner remove someone from a Georgia property?

The owner, an agent, or an attorney in fact signs an affidavit before an officer authorized to administer oaths. The affidavit says the owner claims possession in good faith and that a named person has no good faith claim and still refuses to leave. It goes to the sheriff or a deputy, constable, marshal, or another person certified by the Georgia Peace Officer Standards and Training Council in the county where the land lies.

  • The officer exhibits the affidavit to the occupant at the earliest possible day.
  • Three days after the affidavit was exhibited, the officer turns the occupant out of possession.
  • The occupant may instead hand over a counteraffidavit claiming a good faith legal right to possession, and the officer may administer that oath.
  • With a counteraffidavit, neither party is moved. Both affidavits go to the court clerk for a nonjury trial in magistrate court.
  • If the court finds the counteraffidavit not meritorious by a preponderance of the evidence, the occupant is turned out under a writ of possession as soon as practicable.
  • The court may award the plaintiff fair market rent for the length of the occupancy and other relief it finds appropriate.

Forms and filing details are handled by the magistrate court clerk in your county, so ask that office what it needs. A Georgia attorney can help when facts are disputed, such as a claimed oral lease.

How long must someone occupy land before claiming it?

Twenty years in ordinary cases, or seven years when the possessor holds color of title. The Georgia Department of Revenue course text cites O.C.G.A. 44-5-163 for twenty years and 44-5-164 for seven years, and explains that color of title means a flawed written document, such as a deed from someone who lacked authority to convey.

Time alone does not do it. The Georgia consumer education office lists the elements: actual possession, open and notorious possession, exclusive possession, an uninterrupted period for the entire time the law requires, and a claim of right. It adds that trimming the hedges on a neglected lot next door does not give anyone ownership.

Possession must also be without the true owner's permission, according to the Department of Revenue, and it names government land as traditionally immune from adverse possession. Someone who occupies with the owner's consent, such as a tenant, is not in adverse possession, since consent defeats the claim.

How do the main situations compare?

The table below sets the criminal rule, the removal procedure, and the ownership doctrine side by side. They answer different questions and can overlap in a single dispute.

Georgia squatting, removal and adverse possession rules by source
QuestionGeorgia ruleSource
Is residing without consent an offense?Yes, a misdemeanor under 16-7-21.1House Bill 1017 as passed
How fast must an accused person show documents?Within three business days of the citationHouse Bill 1017 as passed
When can an officer remove an intruder?Three days after the affidavit is exhibited, absent a counteraffidavit44-11-30 as revised by House Bill 1017
Years to claim title without a deedTwenty years44-5-163 in the Department of Revenue course text
Years to claim title with color of titleSeven years44-5-164 in the Department of Revenue course text

Can a person who has held the land for years prove ownership?

Not simply by saying so. The Department of Revenue course text notes that, apart from color of title, an adverse possessor holds no written proof of ownership, and one who tries to sell will probably have difficulty establishing title. The usual route is a quiet title action in which the possessor asks a court to declare ownership, backed by affidavits or witnesses on the length and nature of possession. A judgment can then support later sales.

For an owner, that means a long-running occupation of part of your land, a fence line or an abandoned strip, is worth addressing early. Written permission, a recorded survey, and a conversation with a Georgia attorney protect your title before the period matures.

What should a Georgia owner with an unwanted occupant do before selling?

Start with the paper trail. Gather the deed, any lease or rent receipts, and written notices you sent, because the squatting statute turns on what documents the occupant can produce.

Then decide the route. If the person entered without any permission, the affidavit and removal procedure above, or a report to law enforcement under the unlawful squatting offense, may fit. If the person once had a lease or paid rent, the facts look more like a tenancy, and the Georgia landlord and eviction rules apply instead. Our landlord tenant guide and eviction notice guide cover that path.

Buyers and title companies want a clear occupancy before closing, so removal of the occupant is normally a condition of any sale of the house.

More questions about Georgia Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Can a squatter take ownership of my Georgia house?

Only by meeting every element of adverse possession for the full period: twenty years, or seven years with color of title. The possession must be open, exclusive, uninterrupted, hostile to the owner and under a claim of right.

How quickly can a squatter be removed in Georgia?

Three days after the sheriff or other certified officer shows the owner's affidavit to the occupant, unless the occupant files a counteraffidavit. A counteraffidavit sends the dispute to a nonjury magistrate court trial.

What documents can an accused squatter use?

The statute names a properly executed lease or rental agreement or proof of rental payments, presented within three business days of the citation. If the documents are submitted, a hearing is set within seven days.

Does the owner recover rent from a squatter?

Possibly. If the court finds the counteraffidavit not meritorious, it may award fair market rent for the duration of the occupancy and other monetary relief, and a person whose submitted documents fail at the seven day hearing can face an added fine based on monthly fair market rent.

Does a quitclaim deed give someone ownership after seven years?

Georgia.gov says that is no longer so simple, and more documentation than the deed is required. Seven years applies only when the possessor holds color of title and meets every possession requirement.

What the official sources say

  • Eviction (dispossessory) starts with a demand for possession, then the landlord files a dispossessory affidavit in court; the handbook says the sheriff generally serves it in most counties, and the tenant has 7 days after receiving it to pay the amount or answer. (Georgia Landlord-Tenant Handbook (DCA), dispossessory; source)
  • The sheriff generally supervises the landlord's removal of a tenant who refuses to leave; the landlord bears the cost. (Georgia Landlord-Tenant Handbook (DCA); source)
Selling in Georgia?
We buy Georgia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What written or spoken notice must a Georgia landlord give before an eviction?

A Georgia landlord must first demand that the tenant give up the home, and for unpaid rent the landlord must also hand over a written pay-or-quit notice at least three business days before going to court. The Georgia Landlord-Tenant Handbook from the Department of Community Affairs says the demand itself can be spoken unless rent is the reason, and that no particular wording is required.

A spoken demand is hard to prove later, so the handbook tells landlords to keep a record of when and how they delivered it. The sample it offers is dated, names the tenant and the address, lists the lease term that was broken, and sets a number of days to leave. Whatever the lease says about notice or termination also has to be followed, which makes the lease the first paper to pull out for a landlord or a tenant.

  • The tenant's name and the rental address
  • The date of the notice and the way it was delivered
  • The lease term that was violated, or the rent and fees owed
  • The number of days the tenant has to surrender the home

How does the three business day rent notice work?

The landlord serves a written demand for the back rent and fees, and three business days must pass before a dispossessory case can be filed over money. The handbook says the notice can go out by any method named in the lease, or it can be posted on the unit door in a sealed envelope.

The court affidavit that follows has to say the landlord demanded possession and was refused, and where rent is the reason it has to confirm the three day notice was given. After service of the case papers, the tenant has seven days to pay what the affidavit claims plus court costs. Paying in full ends the case, but the handbook limits this tender defense to once in any twelve month period with the same landlord.

Once a rent case is filed, a landlord normally stops accepting rent so that no payment can be used as a defense. If the case runs longer than two weeks, the landlord can ask the court to order the tenant to pay rent into the court registry while it waits.

How many days does a month-to-month tenancy need to end?

A landlord ending a tenancy at will must give sixty days of notice, and a tenant ending one must give thirty days. The same sixty days applies when a landlord wants to keep the tenant but change the rent amount, since that starts a new tenancy at will.

The handbook also explains how a fixed lease turns into this arrangement. If a lease runs out, the tenant stays, and the landlord keeps taking monthly rent, a tenancy at will arises on the old lease terms, and the sixty and thirty day rules then control. A private landlord does not have to give a reason for declining to renew unless the lease requires one, as long as no discrimination law is broken.

There is a narrow exception on the tenant side. A tenant who holds a court order protecting them or their minor children in a family violence or stalking situation may end a lease on thirty days of notice.

Which Georgia eviction notice or deadline fits each situation?

Georgia landlord and tenant timing as printed in the DCA Landlord-Tenant Handbook (revised 8-29-24) and the Georgia Courts self-help page
SituationNotice or deadlineWho acts
Unpaid rent or feesWritten notice, then three business days before filingLandlord
Other lease violation or holdoverDemand for possession, spoken or writtenLandlord
Ending a tenancy at willSixty daysLandlord
Leaving a tenancy at willThirty daysTenant
Answering the court papersSeven days from actual serviceTenant
Paying rent and costs to stop the caseSeven days after serviceTenant
Moving after a ruling for the landlordWrit requires the tenant to move after seven daysCourt and sheriff

What happens after the notice period ends?

The landlord files a sworn dispossessory affidavit, usually in magistrate court in the county where the rental sits, and the papers are served on the tenant. In most counties the sheriff serves them by handing them to the tenant, giving them to an adult living in the home, or tacking a copy on the door and mailing one.

The tenant then has seven days from actual service to answer, and the clerk will take the answer orally or in writing. When the seventh day lands on a weekend or legal holiday the deadline moves to the next business day. If no answer comes, the court can order the tenant out and send the sheriff, and a default judgment cannot be appealed. Where an answer raises a valid defense, a hearing is usually set within about seven days.

A ruling for the landlord leads to a writ of possession, which is a separate document from the order. The sheriff generally supervises the removal, and the landlord pays for it.

Can a Georgia landlord skip the notice and change the locks?

No. Georgia Courts and the handbook both say a landlord cannot remove a tenant or block access without going through the court process, even when rent is unpaid. A tenant is entitled to stay with active utilities until the court decides.

Georgia also presumes retaliation when a landlord files for eviction, raises rent, cuts services or ends a lease within three months after a tenant asks for repairs, reports a code violation, or takes part in a tenant group. A landlord can rebut that with a lawful reason such as unpaid rent, serious misconduct or a holdover. A tenant who wins a retaliation claim may recover one month of rent plus $500, court costs and possibly attorney fees.

How does an eviction notice affect selling a Georgia house?

It adds steps that a buyer, the owner and the court clerk all need to track, so find out where the case stands before you sign a contract. Ask the magistrate court clerk in the county where the house sits whether a dispossessory case is open, and ask a Georgia attorney whether the lease continues after a sale.

The handbook covers one sale rule: when someone new buys a rental, the former owner must either move the security deposit to the new owner or refund it to the tenant. A tenant who is owed the deposit can sue if neither happens. A person who never had the owner's permission to be on the property is treated differently. The handbook describes that person as a squatter, and an owner can swear an affidavit to have a squatter removed without an eviction case.

Georgia is also a state of homeowners. The Census Bureau lists 11,302,748 residents as of July 1, 2025, an owner-occupied housing rate of 65.7 percent for 2020 to 2024, and a median gross rent of $1,393 for the same years. Rented houses are a real share of what changes hands here, so an as-is buyer should be asked in writing whether the house will be taken with the tenant in place.

More questions about Georgia Eviction Notice Rules

Does a Georgia landlord have to give written notice before evicting?

Only in the rent case. The handbook says a demand to leave can be spoken for most reasons, but a landlord must give written notice to pay at least three business days before filing over unpaid rent or fees. Because a spoken demand is hard to prove, a dated paper copy protects both sides.

How much notice does a month-to-month tenant get in Georgia?

Sixty days. A landlord ending a tenancy at will gives sixty days, and a tenant leaving gives thirty days. The sixty day period also applies to a landlord who wants to change the rent on a month-to-month tenant.

How long does a tenant have to respond once court papers arrive?

Seven days from actual service. A tenant who misses that window can lose by default, and a default judgment cannot be appealed. If the seventh day is a weekend or holiday, the answer is due the next business day.

Can a tenant stop an eviction for unpaid rent by paying?

Yes, once. Paying everything the affidavit claims plus court costs within seven days of service is a complete defense, but a tenant can use it only one time in twelve months with the same landlord. The tenant should also file an answer saying the money was paid or offered.

Does selling the house cancel an eviction notice in Georgia?

Nothing in the handbook says a sale cancels a notice or a lease. It does say the old owner must transfer the security deposit or refund it. Ask the county magistrate court clerk about any open case and consult a Georgia attorney about the lease before closing.
